chunks: Then select for judging between the people the most distinguished of your subjects in your view,
from those whom matters do not vex, disputation does not irritate, he does not persist in error, and he does not grudge turning to the truth when he recognizes it,
and his soul is not prone to greed, and he does not content himself with a superficial understanding without going to its depth,
and he is the most ready to pause on doubtful points among them, the most regardful of arguments, and the least disgusted at the quarrel of litigants,
the most patient at probing into matters, and the most decisive when the judgment becomes clear,
from those whom praise does not make vain, and elation does not make lean (to any side). And those are few.
ai.seo_question: What are the essential moral and intellectual qualities of a judge according to Imam Ali in Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: This passage, part of Imam Ali’s (AS) seminal letter to Malik al-Ashtar, outlines the criteria for selecting a qadi (judge) who possesses not only legal acumen but also the psychological resilience to withstand litigants' pressures and personal biases. In Shia jurisprudence, this highlights the concept of 'Adl' (justice) as an active, discerning virtue requiring both intellectual depth and moral fortitude, ensuring that judicial decisions are rooted in truth rather than convenience or ego. The emphasis on those who are 'least eager to refer back to the opponent' underscores the importance of independent reasoning (ijtihad) and confidence in one's verdict.

en.sayed-ali-raza: (2. The Chief Judge) For the settlement of disputes among people select him who is the most distinguished of your subjects in your view.
The cases (coming before him) should not vex him, disputation should not enrage him, he should not insist on any wrong point, and should not grudge accepting the truth when he perceives it;
he should not lean towards greed and should not content himself with a cursory understanding (of a matter) without going thoroughly into it.
He should be most ready to stop (to ponder) on doubtful points, most regardful of arguments, least disgusted at the quarrel of litigants,
most patient at probing into matters and most fearless at the time of passing judgement.
Praise should not make him vain and elation should not make him lean (to any side). Such people are very few.
